title: Highly multiplexed mammalian metabolic engineering with a shotgun approach - Nature Biotechnology
text:
Download PDF

AbstractMammalian metabolic engineering advances basic biology, bioproduction and cell therapy. However, as pathway complexity increases, so does the size of the combinatorial design space and required DNA constructs, rendering unbiased screens intractable. Here, we developed shotgun genetic engineering (SGE), which exploits the ease of delivering many barcoded small constructs—rather than a single large one—into mammalian cells. Each cell serves as an independent experiment, carrying a synthetic pathway that explores gene content, stoichiometry and organellar localization. Functional pathways are identified by sequencing barcodes from cells exhibiting the desired phenotype. Using SGE, we screened millions of pathway combinations to engineer essential amino acid biosynthesis, achieving near-wild-type growth without valine and enabling isoleucine-free growth in Chinese hamster ovary cells, as well as valine-free growth in Jurkat cells. Functional pathways favored mitochondrial localization and required the integration of tens of kilobases of synthetic DNA, beyond the scale of conventional screening. The resulting datasets support machine-learning-guided decoding and engineering of complex biosynthetic traits in mammalian systems.

MainThe ability to exert precise and predictable control over cellular behavior is a central goal of synthetic biology. In metabolic engineering, this control is often achieved by coordinating the activity of multiple transcription units (TUs), each consisting of a gene and its regulatory elements. Synthetic metabolic pathways are frequently constructed by transplanting coding sequences (CDSs) from diverse species into orthogonal hosts, thereby endowing them with new metabolic capabilities. This approach has yielded notable successes, including the development of cell-based alternatives to industrial manufacturing processes, the stabilization of pharmaceutical supply chains previously dependent on seasonal plant sources and the capture of atmospheric carbon dioxide to generate industrially valuable biomass1,2,3. While these strategies have been extensively demonstrated in microbial chassis, examples of metabolic engineering at this pathway scale in mammalian cells remain rare4,5, despite broad recognition that improved control of mammalian cell function could enhance cell therapies, produce increasingly complex biologics and improve the scalable manufacture of viral vectors6,7,8. Modern DNA synthesis technologies now make it possible to incorporate sequences from across the phylogenetic tree or de novo designed sequences, vastly expanding the functional landscape accessible to mammalian cells.Despite this promise, the limited examples of mammalian metabolic engineering can in part be attributed to the lack of foundational knowledge needed to guide metabolic pathway design. Given a target metabolic pathway and a target host cell type, one is faced with a series of complex design decisions, including the selection of CDSs, the configuration of regulatory elements, the intracellular localization of each encoded protein and the relative expression levels and stoichiometry of each TU required for optimal function (Fig. 1a). These variables create a vast combinatorial design space, yet there is little mechanistic understanding to guide optimal choices.Fig. 1: SGE expands DNA search space to sample many metabolic pathway solutions in parallel.Full size imagea, Metabolic engineering benefits from increasing diversity across the different modules that make up TUs, including promoters, OLSs, enzymatic function, stoichiometry and copy number. b, Classical DBT frameworks in which pathways are tested in succession are inefficient in mammalian cells and other host chassis, which exhibit long doubling times or difficulties associated with engineering or delivering long DNAs that encode more complex biosynthetic pathways. c, SGE increases the scale of metabolic engineering by delivering barcoded individual TUs at high MOI such that each cell carries a unique pathway combination, thereby sampling much more pathway diversity. Following selection, cells displaying the desired phenotype can be sequenced to reveal TU combinations that conferred the desired function. Created in BioRender; Trolle, J. https://biorender.com/43izsew (2026).In fast-growing, genetically tractable microbial systems such as Escherichia coli (20-min doubling time) or Saccharomyces cerevisiae (90-min doubling time), the lack of mechanistic knowledge can often be mitigated through the design–build–test (DBT) framework, where metabolic pathways are rapidly constructed, tested and iteratively refined until satisfactory performance is achieved9,10 (Fig. 1b). Applying similarly complex metabolic engineering strategies in mammalian cells is far more challenging, primarily because of much longer doubling times (typically over 20 h), which drastically slows the pace of iteration.This limitation becomes increasingly severe as pathway complexity grows or as multiple functions are integrated into a single cell. While the final implementation of such complex functions may rely on recent advances in the synthesis and delivery of large DNA constructs to mammalian cells > 100 kb (ref. 11), these approaches are poorly suited for high-throughput screening, as delivering large DNA constructs into mammalian cells is highly inefficient. Modular combinatorial strategies, such as CLASSIC, offer a solution by enabling screening of ~105 constructs at the ~10-kb scale12 (2–3 TUs); however, there is a strong inverse relationship between DNA size and delivery success; it becomes exponentially more difficult to deliver larger constructs, rendering brute-force screening of complex synthetic designs impractical13.To overcome the limitations of experimental screening in mammalian systems, some metabolic engineering approaches incorporate computational screening of candidate interventions before testing in the lab12,14. Sophisticated transcriptomic databases and metabolic models have been developed for commonly used mammalian cell types, enabling the identification of epistatic metabolic functions and the design of complex multiple-knockout cell lines that improve bioprocessing and manufacturability of antibodies15,16,17. However, these models are typically trained on observational data shaped by natural evolution and are optimized for a narrow range of species and cell types commonly used in biomanufacturing. As a result, they are poorly suited for generative design, including scenarios involving the introduction of heterologous or entirely synthetic TUs. The design of TU arrays that comprise synthetic metabolic pathways adds yet another layer of complexity, beyond what these models can currently handle. Thus, synthetic data are needed—systematic, large-scale metabolic perturbations that can be used to train machine learning models capable of predictive and design-oriented applications18.Here, we introduce shotgun genetic engineering (SGE), a multiplexed approach to mammalian metabolic engineering that enables rapid discovery of complex pathway solutions and the creation of large-scale synthetic datasets for training predictive models. SGE leverages high-multiplicity integration of barcoded individual TUs from a pooled library, allowing distinct pathway variants to be randomly assembled within each cell. Because small DNA constructs are exponentially easier to synthesize, assemble and deliver, this design turns each cell into an independent experiment and enables millions of combinations to be screened in parallel. By selecting for cells with desired phenotypes and sequencing their associated barcodes, SGE bypasses the limitations of sequential DBT cycles and dramatically accelerates discovery timelines (Fig. 1c).As proof of concept, we apply SGE to screen millions of pathway combinations for engineering two essential amino acid (EAA) biosynthetic pathways in mammalian cells. In prior work, we enabled Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) cells to proliferate without valine by introducing four E. coli genes, achieving a valine-free doubling time of 3.8 days5. However, we were unable to confer isoleucine independence, despite overlapping biosynthetic steps. Here, we use SGE to both reconstitute and optimize valine prototrophy in CHO cells, yielding clones with a near-wild-type doubling time of just 1.1 days. We also discover a functional six-gene solution enabling isoleucine prototrophy in CHO cells. In both cases, we saw strong signatures favoring mitochondrial localization of biosynthetic enzymes for optimized pathway functionality, indicating that organellar localization is an underexplored variable in mammalian metabolic engineering. Extending this approach, we introduce valine prototrophy to a human T lymphocyte (Jurkat) cell line—an initial demonstration of metabolic pathway expansion in immune cells, with potential applications in engineering stress-resilient cell therapies. Lastly, we show that SGE enables training of a machine learning classifier to identify genetic features predictive of pathway function. Together, these results establish SGE as a scalable framework for pathway-scale metabolic engineering in mammalian cells.ResultsDesign of SGEA central premise of SGE is that individual TUs are exponentially easier to synthesize, assemble and deliver than large multigene constructs. A pooled library of individually barcoded TUs is delivered at high multiplicity of infection (MOI), such that each cell receives a unique combination of pathway components and serves as an independent experiment19. This strategy avoids constructing and delivering each complete pathway individually, enabling scalable exploration of pathway composition, stoichiometry, expression and subcellular localization. To generate TU libraries, barcoded CDSs are synthesized with flanking type IIS restriction sites and directionally cloned into pooled vectors containing barcoded promoters and, where appropriate, N-terminal organellar localization signals (OLSs). Varying promoter strength enables optimization of pathway flux and mitigation of toxicity from pathway components or intermediates20,21,22,23,24, while organellar targeting can increase local enzyme concentrations or provide a favorable biochemical environment1,25. The CDS, promoter and OLS are assembled by Golden Gate cloning into lentiviral-compatible expression vectors, with identifying barcodes positioned within approximately 100 bp of one another in the 3′ untranslated region (UTR) for recovery by a single PCR amplicon.The resulting library is delivered at high MOI, generating cells that vary in TU composition, copy number and stoichiometry. Cells are subjected to a selection or functional screen and enriched pathway configurations are identified by barcode sequencing (Fig. 1c). Although we use growth-based selection here, SGE is compatible with biosensors, fluorescence-activated cell sorting and other functional readouts. Libraries can also incorporate additional CDSs, promoter–OLS pairs, host factor perturbations or alternative delivery mechanisms (for example, transposons or recombinases).We initially selected lentivirus because of the ease of titrating MOI and its broad host range, which allowed us to deploy the same libraries across multiple cell types. However, lentiviral delivery also comes with several practical limitations, including the need to perform packaging after library cloning, constraints on cargo size and potential template switching that can lead to barcode swapping26. Therefore, for some applications, especially when working with larger constructs or when maintaining barcode linkage is essential, a transposon-based strategy (for example, piggyBac) may be more suitable. Additionally, the incorporation of dual 5′ plus 3′ barcoding strategies as used in massively parallel reporter assays27 or direct long-read readouts may help mitigate barcode swapping concerns if lentivirus is to be used.SGE valine/isoleucine library curation and constructionTo confirm the feasibility of SGE as a metabolic engineering approach, we focused on reconstituting EAA biosynthesis in mammalian cells. This challenge offers a stringent test case; EAA biosynthesis was lost in the mammalian lineage over 500 million years ago and mammals must obtain nine amino acids from the environment. In contrast, many microorganisms retain the capacity to synthesize these compounds28,29. Therefore, engineering EAA pathways into mammalian cells presents a powerful model system to explore the boundaries of metabolic rewiring, given its complexity, biotechnological value and experimental tractability. Critically, this system offers a simple and effective selection strategy; cells are grown in the absence of the target amino acid and only those with functional biosynthetic pathways are able to grow5.We initially focused on valine and isoleucine biosynthesis in CHO cells. In previous work, using rational design principles, we found that E. coli ilvN, ilvB, ilvC and ilvD conferred valine prototrophy when expressed at a fixed 1:1:1:1 stoichiometry5(Fig. 2a). However, this same gene set was insufficient to confer isoleucine biosynthesis to CHO cells despite its overlap in enzymatic steps with valine biosynthesis (Fig. 2b). We hypothesized that this might be because of (1) insufficient availability of an isoleucine pathway-specific substrate, 2-oxobutanoate; (2) feedback inhibition of early steps in the pathway by pathway products; or (3) suboptimal catalytic properties of the acetohydroxy acid synthase I (AHAS I) complex encoded by catalytic subunit, ilvB, and regulatory subunit, ilvN.Fig. 2: Engineering BCAA biosynthesis in mammalian cells.Full size imagea, pMTIV pathway designed in a previous study5 to successfully confer valine prototrophy to CHO cells. All genes are derived from E. coli and encoded in a single open reading frame using 2A ribosomal-skipping peptide sequences. ilvN, ilvB, ilvC and ilvD are the subset of genes relevant to valine biosynthesis and were shown to be sufficient to enable valine prototrophy in CHO. b, Pathway map detailing enzymatic steps to enable valine/isoleucine biosynthesis in mammalian cells. Black arrows constitute native mammalian genes. Orange arrows constitute E. coli enzymes previously imported into CHO to enable valine biosynthesis5. Specifically, we added E. coli-derived ilvA to address the hypothesized limitation in the availability of the isoleucine-specific substrate 2-oxobutanoate. To address the second challenge of feedback inhibition, we included two mutant variants of ilvA with partial (ilvAL481F) or complete (ilvAL447F) insensitivity to negative feedback inhibition mediated by isoleucine itself30,31,32. In our previous work, we observed that rationally engineered valine prototrophic CHO cells (pMTIV) grew faster in media with reduced isoleucine concentrations, which we reasoned reflected strong feedback inhibition within the pathway5. Including these variants allowed us to test whether modulating feedback inhibition in a heterologous context could improve pathway function. Lastly, to potentially improve the catalytic properties of the pathway, we added ilvG and ilvM, isozymes of ilvB and ilvN, respectively. Together, ilvG and ilvM form an AHAS II complex, similar to that formed by ilvB and ilvN (AHAS I) but with different catalytic properties—most notably a pronounced (57–180-fold) preference for the isoleucine biosynthetic substrate, 2-oxobutanoate, over the shared isoleucine/valine biosynthetic substrate, pyruvate33,34. AHAS II is furthermore insensitive to feedback inhibition by isoleucine and valine, unlike AHAS I, which responds to inhibition by both amino acids. Lastly, a green fluorescent protein (GFP) CDS was included as a passenger control.Table 1 CDSs included in the SGE library for conferral of isoleucine and valine biosynthesis to mammalian cellsFull size tableEach CDS was paired with either the strong EF1a or medium-strength PGK promoter, with or without a mitochondrial targeting sequence (MTS). Mitochondrial localization was included because compartmentalization can improve pathway function and branched-chain amino acid (BCAA) biosynthesis occurs in the mitochondria of extant eukaryotic prototrophs25,35 (Fig. 2c). Together, the ten CDSs, two promoters and two localization states produced a 40-member TU library. Each promoter–OLS combination and CDS was represented by three barcodes each to distinguish independent integration events.We assembled the library using golden gate cloning (Methods) and performed amplicon-seq to monitor distribution of TUs before viral packaging. There was no greater than a twofold difference in read count between any two TUs within the library, indicating that the library distribution was well balanced with regard to component parts (Extended Data Fig. 1a). The library was packaged in lentivirus and 2.42 million CHO cells were infected at an MOI of 8.8 as estimated by qPCR following infection (Extended Data Fig. 1b).Our choice of ten CDSs, two promoters and two OLSs (40 total TUs) reflected a balance between biological relevance and practical samplability. As we knew four genes to be sufficient to establish a valine prototrophic phenotype, we at a minimum wanted to sample all possible four-TU combinations, of which there are 123,410 from a 40-member library. However, we were interested in sampling variation in copy number as well, motivating a target of sampling all five-TU combinations of which there are 1,086,008. This design space can be sampled within a single 10-cm dish, which we reasoned was appropriate for a pilot-scale demonstration of the approach. Even modest expansions to the library, for example, adding one additional promoter or OLS to yield a 60-TU library, would increase the number of possible five-TU combinations to ~7 million, making comprehensive sampling substantially more challenging in practice. The effective extent to which this combinatorial space is explored can be modeled using a Monte Carlo simulation, as described below.After infection, we performed amplicon-seq to monitor TU distribution and observed underrepresentation of EF1a promoters both with and without MTS (Extended Data Fig. 1a). Because head-to-head comparisons of PGK and EF1a in pooled lentiviral libraries have not been systematically examined before, the basis of this effect remains unclear. In our pooled setting, several mechanisms may contribute to the underrepresentation of EF1a-driven TUs. First, because EF1a is a stronger promoter than PGK, its recruitment of transcriptional machinery could interfere with transcription of the viral genome during packaging, thereby reducing viral titer36,37,38. Second, EF1a contains an intron that is absent from PGK and, although this intron is typically retained during lentiviral packaging, interactions between the intron’s splice sites and the viral splicing and packaging machinery could still modestly impair packaging efficiency39. Lastly, high-level expression driven by EF1a may impose a fitness cost when multiple pathway components are present in the same cell, leading to depletion of EF1a-linked TUs upon infection of the target cells. We also found lesser representation of ilvAL447F (2.6% of reads) and ilvG (1.2% of reads) compared to other CDSs.Monte Carlo simulation to estimate scale of diversity introducedThis imbalance in TU representation prompted us to perform a Monte Carlo simulation to determine whether pathway combinations involving underrepresented TUs were likely to be captured in our infection experiment. We simulated randomized choices of TUs on the basis of the barcode distribution measured for the CHO-Div population at an MOI range of 2–14, assuming a Poisson distribution for integration events. At an MOI of 8, the simulation indicated that we would observe 1.56 million different pathway combinations across the 2.42 million infected cells, with 12.4% of cells encompassing the gene content of our valine biosynthetic pathway (ilvN, ilvB, ilvC and ilvD), while 2.0% of cells would have all four genes localized to the cytoplasm and 1.6% would have all four genes localized to the mitochondria (Extended Data Fig. 1c). We reasoned that this likely constituted sufficient presence of true pathway solutions for us to discover functional valine biosynthetic pathways after selection and proceeded to selection on a valine-restricted medium.More broadly, these simulations illustrate how key experimental parameters such as library size, number of infected cells and MOI jointly determine the fraction of the combinatorial design space that can be sampled in a single screen. Therefore, the achievable coverage can be predicted for any SGE experiment using the same simulation framework, providing a useful starting point for selecting library complexity, MOI and culture scale when designing SGE screens.Reconstitution and optimization of valine prototrophy in CHOCHO-Div was subjected to reduced (4.25 µM) valine medium to favor outgrowth of cells carrying combinations of TUs that together comprised biosynthetic pathways for valine (Fig. 3a). In parallel, we subjected a control population (CHO-GFP) that was transduced with a control virus carrying only GFP to the same selection regimen. After 15 days in low-valine medium, we found clonal outgrowths of cells in the experimental population (CHO-Val) but not in the control CHO-GFP population (Fig. 3b). We picked 16 CHO-Val clones and passaged each individually in a valine-replete (170 µM) medium before characterization using an amino acid dropout assay. As a proxy for cell number, metabolic activity was measured using a resazurin-based reagent40 and valine biosynthetic function was estimated by measuring the ratio of valine-free to valine-replete metabolic activity (Val score). We considered a clone valine prototrophic if its Val score was at least twice that of the parental control. All selected clones (16/16) met this threshold (Fig. 3c). To verify that this functional assay accurately captures valine prototrophic function, we further characterized two clones, CHO-Val-D1 and CHO-Val-D3 (naming convention detailed in the Methods). We cultured both clones in valine-free medium over 10 days, measuring their absolute growth rate. While control cells died off by day 7 in valine-free medium, clones CHO-Val-D1 and CHO-Val-D3 instead proliferated over the 10 days of valine-free culture at rates of 1.14 and 1.05 days per doubling, respectively (Fig. 3d), corresponding to 83% and 80% of their growth rates in valine-replete medium (Extended Data Fig. 2a). Panels a, g, j created in BioRender; Trolle, J. https://biorender.com/43izsew (2026).To further confirm that cells were endogenously synthesizing valine, we cultured CHO-Val-D1 and CHO-Val-D3 in a valine-free ‘heavy’ RPMI medium (Extended Data Fig. 2b and Supplementary Note 1). Both clones exhibited considerably increased 13C2–5 valine labeling at 96.5% and 96.6% respectively, compared to pMTIV cells at 32.2%, indicating strong improvement of the valine biosynthetic phenotype compared to the rationally designed metabolic pathway (Fig. 3e). Indeed, 13C2–5 valine levels detected in clones Val-D1 and Val-D3 matched 13C2–3 alanine levels, suggesting that the engineered biosynthesis of valine in these clones is on par with the native mammalian cellular ability to biosynthesize the non-EAA alanine, which is also biosynthesized from pyruvate.We performed amplicon sequencing to identify the TUs underlying the valine prototrophy phenotype and to characterize genotypic differences between all 16 clones. To distinguish true integration events from background noise, we applied a z-score threshold to TU read counts (Extended Data Fig. 3a). Within each clone, TU barcode counts were grouped into discrete abundance levels consistent with differences in integration copy number, allowing us to estimate that CHO-Val-D1 and CHO-Val-D3 harbor nine and six TU integrations, respectively (Extended Data Fig. 3b). This corresponds to ~37 and ~23 kb of integrated DNA, respectively, or ~19 and ~11 kb of TU modules. In both clones, we found barcodes corresponding to ilvN, ilvB, ilvC and ilvD, consistent with the CDS content of the rationally designed pMTIV pathway with CHO-Val-D3 additionally exhibiting barcode signatures for ilvM, an isozyme of ilvN (Extended Data Fig. 3b). To validate these assignments, we performed long-read sequencing and RNA-seq on CHO-Val-D1 and CHO-Val-D3. Long-read sequencing confirmed TU identities for 38 of 40 calls (Extended Data Fig. 3c,d), while RNA-seq demonstrated that barcode-defined genotypes were largely concordant with transgene expression (Extended Data Fig. 3b,e).Having validated our barcode-based genotyping approach, we next defined genetic configurations underlying valine prototrophy by identifying CDSs present across all prototrophic clones (Val score > 0.28). We found ilvB, ilvC and ilvD presence in every clone exhibiting prototrophy, indicating their necessity in conferring valine biosynthetic function to CHO cells (Fig. 3f); ilvN appeared in 94% (15/16) of clones after selection, suggesting that it strongly supports valine biosynthetic function. This is consistent with prior reports that ilvN acts as a regulatory subunit that enhances ilvB catalytic activity and substrate specificity; ilvB alone retains activity but operates at ~15% of the ilvBN holoenzyme41. In the one clone that lacked ilvN, CHO-Val-D8, cells instead carried its isozyme, ilvM (Supplementary Fig. 1a), suggesting a possible role for a hybrid AHAS holoenzyme ilvBM, which has previously been demonstrated to be functional and demonstrates differential catalytic and feedback properties compared to its canonical AHAS I and AHAS II counterparts41,42.We next sought to determine the optimal promoter and localization context for each CDS by examining TU barcode distributions across promoter–OLS combinations in strongly prototrophic clones (Val score > 0.75). Across 13 such clones, we generated a composite barcode ‘fingerprint’ using the median representation of each TU. Within this fingerprint, mitochondrially localized ilvB, ilvC, ilvD and ilvN expressed from a PGK promoter stood out prominently, defining a pathway ‘solution’ not previously identified through rational design (Fig. 3g). Given that each TU has nine underlying combinatorial barcodes (three barcodes per promoter–OLS combination, three barcodes per CDS), we were able to examine the underlying barcode patterns for each TU within our pathway solution. We found a diversity of barcode patterns underlying each TU among strongly prototrophic valine clones, suggesting that the different clones favored during low-valine selection were derived from multiple independent integration events (Fig. 3h). Across expanded clones, we observed no instances in which ilvN, ilvB, ilvC and ilvD were collectively cytoplasmic, while mitochondrial localization of all four genes was enriched 48-fold relative to expectation according to simulated random TU combinations at an MOI of 8 (Fig. 3i).Although mitochondrially localized PGK-driven ilvAL481F was also represented in the composite barcode fingerprint, we excluded it from the pathway solution because of its overrepresentation in the starting CHO-Div population (Extended Data Fig. 1a). Simulations at MOI = 8 predicted its presence in 59% of clones (Supplementary Fig. 1b), which correlates well with its presence across all valine prototrophic clones, indicating that it is not overrepresented relative to expectation in our screen following selection in reduced valine conditions. Its absence from strongly prototrophic clones CHO-Val-D1 and CHO-Val-D3 further supports this conclusion (Extended Data Fig. 3b).On the basis of these results, we attempted to reconstitute this optimized pathway on a single DNA construct. This design matched our previous pathway, pMTIV, using the same regulatory context and 2A ribosome-skipping peptide sequences (Fig. 2a), but contained mitochondrially localized versions of ilvN, ilvB, ilvC and ilvD. The pathway was synthesized in ~3-kb chunks, assembled using homologous recombination in S. cerevisiae43 and delivered to CHO cells using Flp-In recombination44 (Fig. 3j). The SGE-informed design enabled CHO cells to grow in valine-free RPMI at 1.25 days per doubling, corresponding to 74% of their growth rate in valine-replete conditions, substantially outperforming pMTIV cells (Fig. 3k). Together, these results demonstrate that SGE can uncover functional pathway architectures within vast combinatorial search spaces for complex metabolic engineering challenges and enable their reconstitution on a single DNA construct to confer desired cellular functions.Discovery of metabolic pathway solutions to encode isoleucine prototrophy in CHOTo identify TU combinations that confer isoleucine prototrophy—an outcome we were unable to achieve through rational design—we subjected CHO-Div cells to reduced isoleucine RPMI conditions (1.5, 3 and 6 µM, respectively). In parallel, we subjected a control CHO-GFP population to the same selection regimens. After 15 days in low-isoleucine medium, we found large clonal outgrowths of cells in the experimental populations (CHO-Ile) across all conditions but not in the control CHO-GFP populations. Across the three isoleucine conditions, we picked 46 clones and passaged each individually in an isoleucine-replete (60 µM) medium before performing functional characterization. As previously, we estimated the isoleucine biosynthetic capacity of each clone by measuring the metabolic activity of each clone cultured in isoleucine-free medium and relativizing to metabolic activity in isoleucine-replete medium (Ile score). In total, 41% of clones (19/46) exhibited an improved Ile score relative to the control (Fig. 4a). We further characterized two clones, CHO-Ile-10-H1 and CHO-Ile-10-H2 (naming convention detailed in the Methods), which exhibited strong and intermediate prototrophy, respectively. We cultured both clones in isoleucine-free medium over 10 days and measured absolute cell numbers during this time. While control cells died off by day 6, clone CHO-Ile-10-H1 proliferated over 10 days in isoleucine-free medium at a rate of 1.69 days per doubling, corresponding to 48% of its growth in isoleucine-replete medium, while CHO-Ile-10-H2 initially exhibited a similar growth rate in isoleucine-free medium but tapered off after the eighth day of culture for an overall proliferation rate of 3.04 days per doubling over the 10 days of culture, corresponding to 33% of its growth rate in isoleucine-replete medium (Fig. 4b and Extended Data Fig. 4a).Fig. 4: Discovery of a functional isoleucine biosynthesis pathway in CHO.Full size imagea, PrestoBlue amino acid dropout assay of 46 individual clones selected on low-isoleucine RPMI and the parental control cell line. By leveraging single cells as independent experiments and using random high-copy integration of individual TUs per cell, SGE enables high-throughput assembly and screening of millions of synthetic metabolic pathways. This approach bypasses the inefficiencies associated with building and delivering large DNA constructs, substantially accelerating pathway discovery and optimization.Using this approach, we generated and screened millions of synthetic metabolic pathways to engineer EAA prototrophy in mammalian cells. We achieved (1) near-wild-type growth in valine-free medium and (2) isoleucine prototrophy in mammalian cells. The functional solutions involved integration of 23–52 kb of synthetic DNA—construct sizes impractical to screen using conventional methods. We also provide initial evidence that leveraging organellar compartmentalization can enhance engineered pathway functionality in mammalian cells. Lastly, we demonstrate the versatility of SGE across mammalian cell types (species, in suspension or adhesion) and present a pilot integration with machine learning to predict functional pathway combinations.A consistent theme across the metabolic engineering efforts described here was the preference for mitochondrial localization of BCAA pathway enzymes. This was unexpected given that the genes in our library were sourced from E. coli, a prokaryote lacking subcellular compartments. However, mitochondria are thought to be of bacterial origin and share notable protein composition with bacteria, which may help explain this preference45. Equivalent BCAA biosynthesis genes in extant eukaryotic BCAA prototrophic microbes such as fungi are also localized to mitochondria, providing a clue that there may be biochemical advantages associated with mitochondrial localization, such as increased pyruvate concentrations relative to cytosol46,47 or greater availability of relevant pathway cofactors (for example, iron–sulfur clusters and thiamine diphosphate)25,48,49. Similarly, in plants, these BCAA biosynthetic enzymes are targeted to chloroplasts, which are also an abundant source of pyruvate50. Another possibility is that BCAA biosynthetic enzymes simply benefit from being much more concentrated in a limited organellar physical space, thereby boosting pathway flux and function, as previously demonstrated for other pathways localized to the mitochondria in S. cerevisiae35. This finding highlights the utility of incorporating organellar diversity in the SGE screen and encourages incorporation of yet more organellar targeting signals in future engineering efforts in mammalian cells.Use of SGE comes with several limitations, most notably the requirement for a selectable phenotype. Essential nutrients provide a built-in live–dead screen that effectively identifies cells carrying optimal solutions. However, when the desired phenotype is not linked to cell survival, alternative selection strategies such as coupling pathway activity to fluorescent biosensors, surface marker expression or engineered genetic circuits that connect pathway output to a selectable reporter may be applied51,52. Another limitation of SGE as currently implemented is the use of lentivirus for random integration. We observed substantial biases in TU representation introduced during viral packaging. Specifically, EF1a-driven constructs were markedly underrepresented compared to those with PGK promoters and similar biases were noted for certain CDSs in ways not attributable solely to size. Transitioning to transposon-based delivery systems could alleviate this issue. Lastly, while amplicon-seq can inform what TUs have been integrated in clones of interest, it provides little information about which genes are expressed. In cell lines prone to silencing, this may confound interpretation. Pairing SGE with either bulk or single-cell RNA-seq would provide expression-level information, enabling more accurate assessment of functional pathway configurations.While SGE excels at rapidly exploring vast design spaces through random integration, successful multi-TU solutions identified in this manner may need to be reconstituted into compact, single-vector formats for practical deployment. However, TUs may behave differently when assembled into condensed architectures53. A hybrid strategy may be effective in this case, using SGE for high-throughput discovery, followed by CLASSIC12 or related methods for validation and optimization in compact constructs in lower throughput.Despite its current limitations, SGE represents a powerful strategy for the scalable engineering of increasingly complex biosynthetic traits in mammalian cells.
